title: The Horse and the Groom

full_text:
A wealthy merchant owned a magnificent chestnut stallion of Arabian blood, whose sleek form was the envy of all the neighborhood. The groom in charge of the stables spent hours every day polishing the horse's coat with curry-combs, brushing his mane, braiding his tail with colorful ribbons, and oiling his hooves until they shone like jet.

Yet despite all this meticulous grooming, the poor stallion grew thinner and more haggard day by day; his ribs began to press against his skin, his eyes lost their bright fire, and his knees trembled whenever he was saddled.

The cause was simple: the dishonest groom was secretly stealing the horse's daily rations of oats and sweet barley, selling the grain at the market and pocketing the money, leaving the beast with only moldy chaff and stale straw.

One afternoon, as the groom was lovingly combing the horse's silky neck and whispering lavish compliments, the starving stallion turned his head and spoke with bitter reproach:

"If you truly desire that I should look sleek and handsome, master groom, stop brushing my coat so relentlessly and give me back the oats you steal from my manger! A well-fed horse shines without a comb, but an empty belly starves beneath the finest polish."
moral: Empty grooming and superficial compliments cannot substitute for essential nourishment.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Horse and the Groom"?
options: Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

By running away from every problem
